segments.narration: A spruce forest still stands upright underwater in Kazakhstan. Lake Kaindy, two thousand metres up in the Tian Shan, east of Almaty.
The trunks are Schrenk spruce. Branches and bark stripped away, bleached white, the tops breaking the surface like pale masts. Below, whole trees wait.
Cold mountain water keeps them from rotting. A limestone landslide dammed the gorge and drowned the valley. But when? Guidebooks all said 1911.
Then researchers compared rings from the dead trunks against living spruce on the slopes above. The dead trees stopped growing after autumn 1888.
That points to the Chilik earthquake of July 1889, magnitude 8.2, twenty-two years earlier than anyone thought. The trees dated their own drowning.

verdicts.claim: Lake Kaindy in southern Kazakhstan sits about 2,000 m above sea level and holds a submerged forest of upright spruce trunks.
verdicts.note: 67% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The drowned trees are Schrenk spruce, Picea schrenkiana, and their exposed upper trunks have lost bark and branches and turned white.
verdicts.note: 69% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The lake formed when a limestone landslide dammed the gorge, cold water preserves the trunks, and the event was long attributed to the 1911 Kebin earthquake.
verdicts.note: 80% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: A tree-ring study compared the submerged trunks with living spruce on the surrounding slopes and dated the lake's formation to shortly after autumn 1888.
verdicts.note: The Natural Hazards paper by Miramont, Rizza and colleagues compared ring series from the dead submerged trees with living trees on the surrounding slopes and dated formation to shortly after autumn 1888. The narration says 'then researchers' rather than naming a year, because the record is dated 2024 and the journal issue 2025.

verdicts.claim: That study attributes the lake to the Chilik earthquake of 11 July 1889, magnitude 8.2, about 22 years earlier than the generally accepted date.
verdicts.note: The paper's title and abstract give the 1889 M 8.2 Chilik earthquake, 22 years before the generally accepted date, and confirm the lake lies in its epicentral zone. Other sources put the 1889 magnitude anywhere from 8.0 to 8.3; the narration uses the study's own 8.2.
